description: Great results are promised to those who grind the most.
summary:
Aura-bio, developed by Team Promise, addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health during space missions, when medical support from Earth may be delayed. It brings sensor telemetry, personal baselines, cross-system alerts and daily check-ins into one crew-oriented console.

Instead of treating each reading separately, Aura-bio connects changes in sleep, reaction performance, cardiovascular signals, immune indicators and the spacecraft environment. Alerts explain what changed, show the supporting values and sources, and suggest responses for astronauts and medical teams. Six interactive games support cognitive-performance tracking, while crew-wide notices and lightweight briefings help share important information.

Public NASA and research datasets calibrate the simulator and inform cited limits; all demonstrated crew data is simulated. The prototype also supports local operation without public internet while its server remains available.

Aura-bio matters because crews need understandable, actionable information—not just more measurements. It aims to support onboard awareness and autonomy, while remaining a research prototype rather than a diagnostic medical device.
details:
What Aura-bio does and how it works

Aura-bio, developed by Team Promise, is an astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed for missions where medical support from Earth may be delayed. It helps answer three questions: How am I doing? What changed? What should I do next?**

The system receives sensor and simulated laboratory readings through an MQTT telemetry pipeline. Its backend validates each message, stores it and compares available signals with the astronaut’s personal baseline and configured limits.

Aura-bio connects changes across body systems rather than displaying only isolated measurements. For example, reduced sleep, increased reaction-test lapses and a change in mood can produce one explainable pattern alert. Each alert identifies the contributing values, its urgency, supporting sources and suggested responses for the crew and medical team.

The console includes a clickable body-system map, trends, daily check-ins, crew-wide notices and delayed ground reports. An optional contribution chart explains which signals contribute to the research drift score. Six interactive games—Lunar Alien Reaction, Coloring Shapes, Memory Test, Reaction Test, Speed Click and Number Hunt—provide cognitive-performance activities and session history.

Benefits and intended impact

Aura-bio aims to make health information easier to interpret under demanding mission conditions. Personal baselines provide context for individual differences, while cross-system alerts bring related changes into one explanation.

Crew-wide notices help members stay aware of important developments without replacing their own selected health view. Lightweight briefing files support concise information sharing, and mission presets account for communication delays between the spacecraft and Earth.

The intended impact is stronger onboard awareness and autonomy: helping astronauts and crew medical officers recognize changes, review the evidence and decide when further assessment is needed. These are intended benefits, not demonstrated clinical outcomes.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

We developed the backend in Python, using **]FastAPI** for APIs and WebSocket updates, SQLite for storage, and Mosquitto MQTT with Paho MQTT for telemetry transport.

The web console uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Chart.js for visualization. The games use Python, Pygame and Pygbag/WebAssembly to run in the browser. The research scoring service combines a PyTorch two-day autoencoder for sudden changes with an EWMA drift score for sustained changes.

The hardware pathway uses ESP32 firmware, C/C++, PlatformIO and Wokwi, including simulated sensor and analyzer components. A Serial-to-MQTT bridge connects firmware output to the backend. We used Docker, GitHub, pytest and browser checks for integration and verification.

Data and scientific grounding

Public NASA OSDR Environmental Data Application measurements help calibrate CO₂ variation, while RadLab data informs radiation-dose simulation. Inspiration4 laboratory datasets anchor selected immune-signal ranges and scenario changes. PhysioNet BIDSleep informs normal heart-rate and sleep variation.

Published research and NASA technical references support selected limits and response wording. These sources calibrate the simulation; they do not establish clinical accuracy. All demonstrated crew data is simulated, and optional retimed NASA measurements are explicitly labeled as replayed.

What makes the project creative

Aura-bio’s central idea is to connect signals across systems and present an understandable reason for an alert—not simply a collection of colored numbers. It combines environmental telemetry, physiology, check-ins and interactive games with a shared crew workflow.

Explainability is built into the experience: users can inspect the evidence, distinguish published limits from proposed thresholds, and request deeper model detail without overwhelming the main screen.

Factors our team considered

We considered delayed communication, limited connectivity, individual variation, missing sensors, privacy, readability and alert fatigue. The interface uses urgency words alongside colors, supports dark and light modes, and keeps important status information visible while placing supporting detail behind disclosure controls.

Local game operation does not require public internet once the server and dependencies are available; Wokwi itself remains an online service. Missing measurements are not shown as healthy.

We also prioritized honest limitations. Aura-bio is not a medical device. Physical-device calibration, independent clinical validation and real OS/mobile push verification remain future work. Metabolic measurements are not yet implemented, and the radiation/immune pattern requires a configured dose threshold before it can trigger.
